# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure worldwide [1]. For decades, neurohormonal blockade with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) formed the cornerstone of therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift by simultaneously augmenting beneficial natriuretic peptide signaling and inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system [3].

## Pharmacology and Mechanism

Sacubitril/valsartan is a supramolecular sodium salt complex combining the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril (AHU377) with the angiotensin receptor blocker valsartan [4]. Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [5]. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril increases circulating natriuretic peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and antifibrotic effects, while valsartan blocks the deleterious effects of angiotensin II [6]. Because neprilysin inhibition alone increases angiotensin II, combined receptor blockade is essential [7]. Earlier attempts to combine neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition (omapatrilat) were abandoned because of unacceptable rates of angioedema attributable to bradykinin accumulation [8].

## Pivotal Clinical Evidence in HFrEF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8442 patients with HFrEF (NYHA class II–IV, ejection fraction ≤40%, later ≤35%) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [9]. The trial was stopped early for benefit: sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, with significant reductions in all-cause mortality [9]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and progressive pump failure, as well as a slowing of renal function decline [10,11]. Quality of life and symptom burden also improved compared with enalapril [12]. Sacubitril/valsartan was associated with more hypotension but less hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction, with low rates of angioedema [9].

Real-world registries and the TRANSITION and PIONEER-HF studies extended these findings, showing that initiation during or shortly after hospitalization for acute decompensated HF was safe and lowered NT-proBNP levels more effectively than enalapril [13,14]. PIONEER-HF further demonstrated reductions in HF rehospitalization with in-hospital initiation [14]. The PROVE-HF study linked NT-proBNP reductions with favorable cardiac reverse remodeling, including improvements in ejection fraction and ventricular volumes [15].

## Heart Failure with Preserved and Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction

The role of ARNI in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is less definitive. The PARAGON-HF trial randomized patients with ejection fraction ≥45% to sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan and narrowly missed its primary endpoint of reducing total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death [16]. Prespecified subgroup analyses suggested possible benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction (≤57%) and in women [17,18]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF supported a treatment effect that attenuated with increasing ejection fraction [19]. These data informed guideline recommendations extending consideration of ARNI to patients with mildly reduced ejection fraction [20].

## Guideline Recommendations

Contemporary guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Failure Society of America and the European Society of Cardiology recommend ARNI as a preferred renin-angiotensin system inhibitor in HFrEF, as one of the four foundational ("quadruple therapy") drug classes alongside beta-blockers, MRAs, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors [20,21]. Guidelines emphasize early initiation and rapid sequencing of these therapies [22]. A 36-hour washout from ACEIs is required to minimize angioedema risk [21].

## Practical Considerations and Safety

Initiation requires attention to blood pressure, renal function, and potassium [23]. Symptomatic hypotension is the most common adverse effect, particularly in older and lower-weight patients [24]. Angioedema is rare but more frequent in patients of African ancestry [9]. Sacubitril/valsartan modestly raises natriuretic peptides, so BNP—but not NT-proBNP—becomes unreliable for monitoring [25]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have generally found ARNI to provide reasonable value relative to ACEIs in HFrEF [26]. Despite proven efficacy, real-world uptake and dose titration remain suboptimal, reflecting clinical inertia, tolerability concerns, and cost barriers [27,28].

## Emerging Directions

Ongoing research explores ARNI effects on atrial fibrillation, post-myocardial infarction remodeling, and combination with newer agents [29]. The PARADISE-MI trial did not demonstrate significant superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over ramipril after acute myocardial infarction, tempering enthusiasm for that indication [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed HFrEF management by delivering robust reductions in mortality and hospitalization, supported by evidence of reverse remodeling. Its role in HFpEF remains nuanced, with benefit concentrated at the lower end of the ejection fraction spectrum. Continued efforts to improve implementation and titration are needed to realize its full population-level benefit.
